query: How much can the choice of simulated user change the results of an AI agent benchmark, and what mistake do simulated users make most often?
summary:
Research Objective:
Determine how much the choice of simulated user affects AI agent benchmark results and identify the most common user-simulator errors. [2609.38043v1]

Methodology:
Researchers introduced UserProxyBench, an evaluation layer over the τ-bench family, and the User Fidelity Score (UFS), which measures adherence to the benchmark's private user instructions using task-grounded rubric criteria scored independently of agent success. They held the agent fixed at GPT-5.5 and varied only the user proxy across 375 enterprise tasks, evaluating seven different proxies over 2,618 scored trajectories. [2609.38043v1]

Key Findings:
Holding the agent fixed and varying only the simulated user changed mean task reward by 15.2 points, with mean Rτ ranging from 0.644 to 0.796 across proxies. Per-domain spread (excluding Banking) ranged from 0.132 to 0.298, reaching 0.280 on Airline and 0.298 on Retail. Across all trajectories, 24.4% of agent-successful episodes failed UFS; on Telecom, 39.7% of all trajectories were Rτ pass / UFS fail. The dominant failure was premature disclosure: users provide information before it is requested. This behavior had little effect on task reward, yet among successful episodes it caused the agent to make 1.06 fewer tool calls on average, changing the interaction being evaluated while preserving the reward. Across seven proxies, an empirical cost-fidelity frontier was identified, enabling practitioners to select the least expensive simulator that satisfies a required fidelity level. [2609.38043v1]

query: Can an AI model's step-by-step reasoning be trusted as a record of how it reached its answer?
summary:
Research Objective:
Determine whether correct answers from language models are reliably accompanied by valid chain-of-thought reasoning traces, and whether trace properties such as minimality and coherence indicate genuine reasoning. [2609.38107v1]

Methodology:
Researchers used iGSM, a synthetic grade-school mathematics benchmark that exposes the exact quantities and dependencies a correct solution should use, enabling programmatic step-by-step verification of generated traces. They first evaluated a clean model trained exclusively on valid, minimal traces. They then intervened on trace supervision: training on valid but non-minimal traces, re-asking the same problem with a different query, swapping traces between unrelated problems, and randomly shuffling 10% of tokens in training trace sentences. [2609.38107v1]

Key Findings:
On the hardest problems (op=23), 31.6% of correct answers were accompanied by invalid traces. Over half of these invalid traces (51.2% at op=23) passed all syntactic and arithmetic checks but failed semantic dependency checks. Answer correctness and trace validity nearly coincided in distribution but diverged sharply out of distribution. Models trained on swapped traces still answered 82% of in-distribution problems correctly despite never emitting a valid trace. Models trained on 10%-shuffled traces nearly preserved clean-model accuracy even out of distribution, with no generated trace passing verification. Minimality was strongly shaped by supervision and query placement; re-asking the same problem about a different quantity revealed computations inherited from the original query, showing minimality alone does not establish independent planning. Computational usefulness and trace validity are distinct properties. [2609.38107v1]

Limitations:
The authors state that their models are small and synthetic, so direct extrapolation to frontier systems is unwarranted. [2609.38107v1]

summary:
Research Objective:
Determine whether step-by-step reasoning traces (chain-of-thought) can be trusted as faithful records of how models derive their answers, and develop methods to verify and monitor such traces. [2609.38107v1, 2609.37203v1, 2610.00601v1]

Methodology:
Three complementary approaches were used. First, researchers created iGSM, a synthetic grade-school mathematics benchmark where the exact quantities and dependencies of a correct solution are known, enabling programmatic step-by-step verification of generated traces (syntactic, arithmetic, and semantic dependency checks). They evaluated models trained on clean minimal traces, non-minimal traces, swapped traces (between unrelated problems), and traces with 10% token-level shuffling. [2609.38107v1] Second, they proposed Proof-R1, a reinforcement learning framework that uses UNSAT-based machine-checkable formal verification (MCFV) to admit conclusions into a verified proof state only when reasoning actions satisfy proof obligations, and recovers the answer-supporting dependency closure (ASDC) to trace the proof structure. [2609.37203v1] Third, they introduced TRUST, an offline-trained value model that predicts eventual reasoning correctness from partial CoT prefixes, using it to monitor and selectively steer reasoning generation in frozen vision-language-action (VLA) policies (Alpamayo 1.5 and DeepThinkVLA). [2610.00601v1]

Key Findings:
On iGSM, answer correctness and trace validity nearly coincide in distribution but decouple under distribution shift: on the hardest problems (op=23), 31.6% of correct answers are accompanied by invalid traces, and 51.2% of those invalid traces pass all syntactic and arithmetic checks while failing semantic dependency checks. [2609.38107v1] Models trained on swapped traces still achieve 82% in-distribution accuracy despite never emitting a valid trace; models trained on 10% token-shuffled traces nearly preserve clean-trace accuracy even out of distribution, again with no generated trace passing verification. [2609.38107v1] Non-minimal training traces induce non-minimal outputs, and re-asking the same problem with a different query reveals computations inherited from the original query, showing minimality alone is insufficient evidence of selective planning. [2609.38107v1] Proof-R1 improves answer accuracy across three logical reasoning benchmarks and four backbone models while outperforming baselines in reasoning-process verifiability. [2609.37203v1] TRUST monitors reasoning correctness with 88.9% accuracy on Alpamayo 1.5, improves reasoning correctness from 75.9% to 90.0%, reduces collision rate by 30.4% and maximum trajectory error by 11.5% on a challenging subset; on DeepThinkVLA it improves grasp-state claim correctness from 69.3% to 90.2% and action-choice claim correctness from 68.8% to 85.9%, yet closed-loop task performance on LIBERO-Plus remains largely unchanged, demonstrating that correctability does not guarantee actionability. [2610.00601v1]

Limitations:
The iGSM experiments use small synthetic models, so direct extrapolation to frontier systems is unwarranted. [2609.38107v1] Proof-R1 evaluates only a controlled subset of natural-language reasoning (English benchmarks with well-defined deductive structures), abstracting away linguistic ambiguity, implicit background knowledge, and pragmatic interpretation, and does not exhaust the broader reasoning landscape. [2609.37203v1] TRUST's correctness metric depends on a VLM judge; the value model is trained on unsteered rollouts while steering changes the reasoning distribution, risking distribution shift; and TRUST-based steering adds approximately 81% inference time overhead relative to unsteered Alpamayo 1.5. query: Do AI agents actually carry out the plans they say they will follow?
summary:
Research Objective:
Investigate whether LLM agents preserve the planning structure they declare, whether planning-pattern effectiveness varies across environments and models, and whether matching a declared planning pattern to a corresponding pattern-specific executor improves task success. [2609.38108v1]

Methodology:
Researchers evaluated agents built on three LLM families (Qwen3.6, DeepSeek-V4, Gemma-4-26B) across four benchmarks: WebArena, Mind2Web, SWE-Bench Verified, and ALFWorld. They compared three conditions: (i) a no-planning Flat ReAct baseline, (ii) a plan-prompted Flat ReAct baseline (Plan+ReAct), and (iii) the Planning-as-Routing framework, in which the LLM declares one of four planning modes (Predefined, Sequential, Hierarchical, or Search) and a deterministic router dispatches the task to the corresponding pattern-specific executor. They measured plan quality, plan adherence, structural faithfulness, and task success. [2609.38108v1]

Key Findings:
Generic Plan+ReAct preserved declared planning structures in only 22–45% of trajectories across three benchmarks, with structural fidelity decreasing as plans became longer; pattern-specific executors enforced the intended structure. Planning-mode effectiveness varied by environment and model: Search performed best on ALFWorld, Hierarchical on SWE-Bench Verified, and the strongest pattern could differ across models within the same benchmark. Pattern-specific executors improved task success from 0.48 to 0.92 on ALFWorld and from 0.36 to 0.44 on SWE-Bench Verified over Plan+ReAct. Retry-matched controls indicated that forced-pattern oracle gains largely reflected additional execution attempts rather than task-specific pattern complementarity. Current LLMs did not reliably select the strongest mode for each task, though few-shot demonstrations improved selection more consistently than enabling thinking in some benchmark–model combinations. [2609.38108v1]

Limitations:
The study considers four planning patterns and task-level routing under fixed execution budgets. Future work could extend the framework to additional or dynamically composed planning strategies, allow agents to switch modes during execution, and evaluate structural fidelity jointly with action correctness, execution cost, and recovery behavior. Detailed limitations are discussed in Appendix M. [2609.38108v1]

query: How consistent is gender bias across different AI language models, and how should a company check for it?
summary:
Research Objective:
Determine how consistent gender bias is across different AI language models and how companies should approach bias auditing. [2609.38036v2]

Methodology:
Researchers evaluated ten models released between April 2025 and June 2026 from nine vendors using two paradigms: Study 1 measured gender attribution to stereotyped phrases, and Study 2 measured moral judgment of abuse or torture against a woman or a man to prevent a catastrophic outcome. [2609.38036v2]

Key Findings:
Eight of ten models showed a significant gender-related asymmetry in at least one study. In Study 1, two models (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Mistral Small 4) showed a significant asymmetry in the direction IM > IF (attributing masculine-stereotyped phrases to female writers more often), three models (Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek V4-Flash, Qwen3.6) showed the opposite pattern (IF > IM), and five models showed no significant effect. In Study 2, six models (Grok 4.1 Fast, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.5, Qwen3.6, Claude Fable 5) converged on a male-disadvantaging asymmetry, judging abuse of a man as more acceptable than abuse of a woman, while three other models showed no variation across conditions. The direction and magnitude of gender bias are highly heterogeneous across models, with some models behaving in diametrically opposite ways. The authors conclude that bias auditing should be treated as an ongoing, multi-vendor process rather than a one-time assessment. [2609.38036v2]

query: How can a company estimate how confident an AI model is in its own answer?
summary:
Research Objective:
Investigate methods for estimating an AI model's confidence in its own answers, including whether confidence estimates reliably reflect the model's knowledge state and generalize as knowledge evolves. [2609.38797v1, 2610.01006v1, 2609.39518v1, 2609.37647v1, 2609.37993v1]

Methodology:
Multiple approaches were evaluated across five studies. Researchers tested Self-Consistency (SC) using beam search (beam size 10) with NLI-based answer grouping to estimate generation probabilities on open-model checkpoints [2609.38797v1]. They introduced knowledge contrast sets—subsets where one checkpoint answers correctly and another incorrectly—to measure persistent calibration across model updates [2609.38797v1]. A controlled audit of the decision model Jev used paired interventions varying information supply while holding items fixed, comparing confidence against follow-up questions about whether an outcome is settled, whether evidence suffices, and whether the model knows the answer [2610.01006v1]. In a human–AI collaboration puzzle task, elicited belief distributions over candidate pieces were compared to raw action-token probabilities across three frontier vision-language models (GPT-4.1, GPT-5, GPT-5.5) and a human study (N=210) [2609.39518v1]. Jev (jev-1.13.0) was benchmarked zero-shot on 37 datasets (346,009 requests) against Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma-4-E4B, evaluating calibration and selective prediction [2609.37647v1]. An agentic RAG pipeline (BITEM at NTCIR-19 R2C2) computed confidence from orchestrator-recorded signals—search counts, entailment cascade scores, verification passages, and deliberation length—without asking the model to rate itself [2609.37993v1].

Key Findings:
Self-Consistency with beam search and NLI grouping provides a practical inference-time confidence estimator [2609.38797v1]. On knowledge contrast sets, both inference-time and fine-tuning methods fall short of oracle methods trained on future checkpoints, even when well-calibrated on the full dataset; multi-checkpoint training improves contrast-set calibration, suggesting a path to robust meta-knowledge features [2609.38797v1]. Jev's confidence is calibrated on familiar closed-choice tasks (SmoothECE 0.015–0.033) and supports selective prediction (e.g., at 50% coverage accuracy rises from 79.7% to 96.3% on Banking77), but fails as an indicator of missing knowledge: with no answer-relevant information it assigns up to 0.80 to a salient option, and on news beyond an observed knowledge boundary confidence exceeds accuracy by 0.21–0.33 [2610.01006v1, 2609.37647v1]. Targeted follow-up questions give sharper readouts: "is the outcome settled" achieves AUROC 1.00, "does evidence suffice" achieves 0.95 (vs. 0.85 for confidence on same items), while "do you know?" mostly reads surface cues (realistic names, dates) [2610.01006v1]. Elicited belief distributions are better calibrated (ECE 0.15) and discriminate correct from incorrect placements better (AUROC 0.65) than raw action-token probabilities (mean confidence 0.97, ECE 0.44); however, models seldom externalize uncertainty, asking for clarification on only 3.5–16.7% of turns [2609.39518v1]. In the agentic RAG pipeline, single-pass confidence carried no information about correctness (AUROC 0.463), while orchestrator-computed confidence from multi-pass traces improved HMR from 0.2719 to 0.4915 and accHMR from 0.2464 to 0.4531; hand-crafted rules on the same signals further raised accuracy to 0.9375 and HMR to 0.6985 [2609.37993v1].

Limitations:
[2610.01006v1] Scope limited to one version of one closed model (Jev); surface-cue controls evaluated on curated contrasts with text-only baselines; date removal may change question propositions; knowledge boundary is an observational accuracy change point, not a verified training cutoff; most benchmarks converted to forced-choice multiple choice; follow-up answers validated as rankings, not calibrated probabilities; cost-based utility and complete deployment routing policy not evaluated; some exploratory analyses reused the same dated-news panel. [2609.37647v1] Single prompt template per dataset without tuning; reference models (Qwen, Gemma) scored with prompts written for Jev and without reasoning; allowing reasoning LLMs to reason would likely raise accuracy at higher cost. [2609.37993v1] Test set of only 64 questions; rules chosen on held-out halves but may be properties of that specific set; hand-written rules not yet validated on unseen question sets; running four passes costs ~4× single pass. [2609.38797v1] The provided research content does not specify limitations. [2609.39518v1] The provided research content does not specify limitations.

Methodology:

query: How can a company estimate how confident an AI model is in its own answer?
summary:
Research Objective:
Investigate methods for estimating an AI model's confidence in its own answers, including calibration evaluation, persistent calibration across evolving model knowledge, behavioral audits distinguishing confidence from knowledge gaps, elicited uncertainty in human–AI collaboration, and pipeline-derived confidence signals. [2609.38797v1, 2610.01006v1, 2609.39518v1, 2609.37647v1, 2609.37993v1]

Methodology:
[2609.38797v1] Evaluated confidence estimation methods — Self-Consistency (beam search size 10 with NLI grouping of equivalent answers) and LoRA + Verbalized Confidence — on sequences of model checkpoints. Used knowledge contrast sets (questions where one checkpoint answers correctly and another incorrectly) to test persistent calibration. Compared non-oracle training on early checkpoints [C1, C2] against oracle training on later checkpoints [C3, C4]. [2610.01006v1] Audited Jev, a decision model, across 15+ public datasets and 6 generated task families using paired interventions that vary supplied information for fixed items. Measured calibration (SmoothECE) and follow-up questions (whether an outcome is settled, whether evidence suffices, whether the model knows the answer) with AUROC. [2609.39518v1] Compared elicited belief distributions over candidate pieces against raw action-token probabilities in a collaborative puzzle task. Tested four communication conditions (Generic, Described, Hedged, Self-hedged) with three frontier vision-language models (GPT-4.1, GPT-5, GPT-5.5) and a controlled human study (N=210). [2609.37647v1] Evaluated Jev zero-shot on 37 datasets (346,009 requests) with one frozen template per dataset. Analyzed calibration and selective prediction (accuracy vs. coverage curves) and compared with Qwen3.8-27B and Gemma-4-E4B on identical prompts. [2609.37993v1] Built an agentic RAG pipeline where an orchestrator computes confidence from pipeline signals (verified passages, entailment cascade scores, reasoning length) without model self-rating. Ran multiple retrieval passes, pooled results, and crafted hand-written rules to improve confidence estimates.

Key Findings:
[2609.38797v1] Self-Consistency achieved ECE values of 0.333, 0.741, 0.873; non-oracle training 0.476, 0.821, 0.871; oracle training 0.506, 0.855, 0.888. Multi-checkpoint training improves contrast-set calibration, but substantial headroom remains due to a vast space of checkpoint-specific confidence features. [2610.01006v1] Jev is calibrated on familiar closed-choice tasks (SmoothECE 0.015–0.033) but fails as a missing-knowledge indicator: with no information it assigns 0.80 to a salient option; on post-boundary news confidence rises to 0.82 while true accuracy is 0.51–0.52. Follow-up questions detect gaps: settled AUROC 1.00, enough 0.95, known 0.91 — but known relies on surface cues (realistic names, dates). [2609.39518v1] Elicited belief distribution is better calibrated (ECE 0.15) and discriminates correct/incorrect placements (AUROC 0.65) versus raw action-token probabilities (mean confidence 0.97, ECE 0.44). Human study: Generic condition accepts 78.3% of wrong moves; Hedged condition reduces wrong-move acceptance to 36.4% with discrimination 27.7/37.3 pp; Self-hedged condition accepts 50.2% of wrong moves. [2609.37647v1] Jev reaches 95–99% accuracy on IMDB, SST-2, HellaSwag, ARC and 86.7% on Belebele.

query: How can the memory and compute cost of running long-context language models be reduced without losing accuracy?
summary:
Research Objective:
Investigate methods to reduce the memory and compute cost of running long-context language models while maintaining or improving accuracy across diverse tasks and model architectures. [2610.02687v1, 2609.36935v2, 2609.37988v2, 2609.39358v1, 2610.02070v2]

Methodography:
Five distinct approaches were evaluated. GraphMemory organizes procedural knowledge as a graph and retrieves only query-relevant subgraphs, bounding retrieved content per query. [2610.02687v1] CoEM (Commit-on-Evidence Memory) preserves source excerpts verbatim in a pending set until later context clarifies relevance, then uses a frozen NLI verifier to commit only supported facts. [2609.36935v2] KV-Kaizen learns a per-layer selector that chooses depth-sharing, precision-reduction, and rank-truncation actions under a global cache budget during supervised fine-tuning. [2609.37988v2] Galahad adds a memory layer to vLLM, SGLang, and llama.cpp: Taliesin stores and reloads exact KV-cache blocks by byte-identical match, while Blaise indexes documents and passes only the needed section to the model. [2609.39358v1] Causal Memory Policy (CMP) intervenes on retrieval itself with known propensities, using self-normalized inverse propensity weighting to estimate memory utility when deterministic retrieval leaves memories unobserved. [2610.02070v2]

Key Findings:
GraphMemory reduces memory-construction tokens by 81–85%, test-time tokens by 78.6%–92.2%, and estimated API cost similarly, while maintaining competitive accuracy on FINER and FORMULA financial reasoning tasks with Claude Haiku 4.5 and Qwen3.8-27B. [2610.02687v1] CoEM consistently outperforms memory baselines; with Qwen3.5-9B it leads by 10.4–11.4 F1 points at 6,400 documents, and its answer F1 declines only 1.0–2.1 points across 50–6,400 documents versus 9.6–11.3 for ReMemR1. The policy generalizes to 2WikiMultiHopQA and MuSiQue without retraining. [2609.36935v2] KV-Kaizen reaches the Pareto frontier of accuracy vs. cache size: a 4× cache reduction incurs no accuracy degradation from 7B parameters up, and combining 4× representation compression with token eviction yields a 32× smaller decode-time cache on a 14B model while preserving accuracy. Learned configurations outperform static, random, and search-based baselines. [2609.37988v2] Galahad makes LLM reading a one-time cost: on seven real-world datasets 98.7% of prompt tokens were previously read text. On a 97,000-token recall test with Gemma 4 31B, Taliesin alone answered 98/100 at 3.0 s/572 J vs. 10/100 at 9.3 s/2,754 J without Galahad; adding Blaise achieved 100/100 at 0.59–0.64 s and 200–213 J across all three runtimes. Restored KV state is bit-identical (262,144 logits matched). Galahad worked on 30/30 tested models. [2609.39358v1] CMP reveals that deterministic retrieval leaves memory utility unidentified for 54% of required memories on LongMemEval and 67% on LoCoMo; CMP improves discrimination between required and non-required memories from 0.54 to 0.66 AUC. However, per-query utility (0.78 AUC) does not aggregate to predict value on unseen queries. [2610.02070v2]

Limitations:
GraphMemory results are preliminary, covering two related financial tasks, two models, and one primary baseline (ACE); broader evaluations, additional baselines, and repeated runs are needed. Retrieval overhead makes individual test queries slower despite lower token usage, motivating embedding-based/hybrid retrievers, caching, and improved graph routing. Longer continual-learning streams and cross-model transfer remain untested. [2610.02687v1] KV-Kaizen requires specialized kernels to realize memory/speed benefits of mixed widths and bit-widths across layers; rank compression needs MLA conversion with varying accuracy cost; budget conditioning depends on training targets, and widening their range can reduce accuracy even at less compressed settings. [2609.37988v2] The provided research content does not specify limitations for CoEM, Galahad, or CMP.

summary:
Research Objective:
Reduce the memory and compute costs of running long-context language models while preserving or improving reasoning accuracy. The retrieved papers address this through five complementary approaches: structured graph-based memory with bounded retrieval (GraphMemory), delayed evidence commitment with verification (CoEM), learned per-layer KV-cache compression (KV-Kaizen), byte-exact KV-state and document reuse (Galahad), and causal identification of memory utility under retrieval positivity violations (CMP). [2610.02687v1, 2609.36935v2, 2609.37988v2, 2609.39358v1, 2610.02070v2]

Methodography:
GraphMemory organizes procedural knowledge as a graph and retrieves only query-relevant subgraphs, keeping retrieved memory constant as examples grow; evaluated on FINER and FORMULA financial tasks with Claude Haiku 4.5 and Qwen3.8-27B. [2610.02687v1]
CoEM maintains a bounded pending set of verbatim source excerpts, promotes them to committed memory only after a frozen NLI verifier confirms support, and trains the promotion policy via reinforcement learning with step-level evidence rewards; tested on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue with Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-4B. [2609.36935v2]
KV-Kaizen learns a context-adaptive selector that chooses per-layer depth sharing, precision reduction, and rank truncation under a global cache budget; the selector runs once before pre-fill and the model is trained under the chosen configuration; evaluated on IFEval and GSM8K with Qwen2.5-7B and long-context tasks with 14B models. Key Findings:
GraphMemory reduces memory-construction tokens by 81–85%, test-time tokens by 78.6%–92.2%, and estimated API cost similarly while maintaining competitive accuracy across two financial tasks and two LLM backbones. [2610.02687v1]
CoEM outperforms the strongest memory baseline by 10.4–11.4 F1 points at 6,400 documents with Qwen3.5-9B; its answer F1 declines only 1.0–2.1 points across 50–6,400 documents versus 9.6–11.3 for ReMemR1, and it beats general-purpose LLMs by 17.5–21.0 F1 points at 1,600 documents. KV-Kaizen achieves a 4× cache reduction with no accuracy degradation from 7B parameters upward, and a 32× smaller decode-time cache on a 14B model when combined with token eviction while preserving accuracy. query: How can the memory and compute cost of running long-context language models be reduced without losing accuracy?
summary:
Research Objective:
Reduce the memory and compute cost of running long-context language models while preserving or improving reasoning accuracy. The retrieved papers address this through structured external memory systems that retrieve only relevant content [2610.02687v1], delayed-commitment memory policies that preserve unresolved evidence until its relevance is clarified [2609.36935v2], learned per-layer KV-cache compression across depth, precision, and rank dimensions [2609.37988v2], byte-exact KV-state persistence and document-section retrieval to make reading a one-time cost [2609.39358v1], and causal retrieval randomization to identify true memory utility [2610.02070v2].

Methodology:
GraphMemory organizes procedural knowledge as a graph and retrieves a bounded, query-relevant subgraph for each query, keeping retrieved tokens constant as processed examples grow; evaluated on FINER (1,000/500/441 train/val/test) and FORMULA (500/300/200) with Claude Haiku 4.5 and Qwen3.8-27B [2610.02687v1]. CoEM maintains a pending set of verbatim source excerpts under a fixed context-memory budget, uses a learned policy trained with reinforcement learning (step-level evidence rewards plus final answer rewards) to promote, retain, or discard excerpts, and employs a frozen NLI verifier to admit only source-supported facts; tested on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue with Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-4B [2609.36935v2]. KV-Kaizen learns a selector during supervised fine-tuning that chooses per-layer cache configurations across three axes—sharing caches across layers (depth), reducing bits per entry (precision), and truncating low-rank latent representations (rank)—under an overall compression budget; evaluated on instruction following (IFEval) and reasoning (GSM8K) with Qwen2.5 models from 0.5B to 14B [2609.37988v2]. Galahad adds two memory layers to vLLM, SGLang, and llama.cpp: Taliesin saves and reloads exact KV state for byte-identical text blocks, and Blaise stores documents and passes only the relevant section to the model; tested on a 97,000-token corpus with 100 hidden facts using Gemma 4 31B, and on seven real-world datasets [2609.39358v1]. CMP reserves a fixed number of context slots for memories sampled with known propensities, estimates utility via self-normalized inverse propensity weighting under a balanced assignment design, and proves identification, unbiasedness, and the optimal decision rule; evaluated on LongMemEval and LoCoMo, and in a deployed Mem0 system [2610.02070v2].

Key Findings:
GraphMemory reduces memory-construction tokens by approximately 81–85%, estimated API cost by a similar margin, and test-time tokens by 78.6%–92.2% while maintaining competitive accuracy across three dataset–model configurations [2610.02687v1]. CoEM consistently outperforms memory baselines; with Qwen3.5-9B the margin over the strongest baseline grows from 1.3–2.1 F1 at 50 documents to 10.4–11.4 F1 at 6,400 documents, and answer F1 declines only 1.0–2.1 points across that range versus 9.6–11.3 for ReMemR1; at 1,600 documents CoEM leads general-purpose LLMs by 17.5 F1 on HotpotQA and 21.0 F1 on 2WikiMultiHopQA and MuSiQue [2609.36935v2]. KV-Kaizen reaches the Pareto frontier of accuracy versus cache size: at 4× cache reduction there is no accuracy degradation from 7B parameters up; combining 4× representation compression with token eviction yields a 32× smaller decode-time cache on a 14B model with significant accuracy preserved; a compressed larger model is more accurate than a smaller uncompressed model with the same cache size [2609.37988v2]. Galahad’s Taliesin alone let a model attend to the full 97,000-token corpus and answer 98 of 100 recall questions on llama.cpp at 3.0 s and 572 J per question, versus 10 of 100, 9.3 s and 2,754 J without Galahad (limited to last 12,000 tokens); adding Blaise achieved 100 of 100 on all three runtimes at 0.59–0.64 s and 200–213 J; corpus storage is a one-time cost of ~100 s and 28 kJ, recovered after 13 questions; restored KV state is bit-identical (all 262,144 logits matched) and worked on 30 of 30 tested models [2609.39358v1]. CMP reveals that identification fails for 54% of required memories on LongMemEval and 67% on LoCoMo under deterministic retrieval, and this failure persists in a deployed Mem0 system; CMP improves discrimination between required and non-required memories from 0.54 to 0.66 AUC; however, per-query utility reaches 0.78 AUC only for the query on which it is estimated, and no available aggregation predicts a memory’s value on unseen queries [2610.02070v2].

Limitations:
GraphMemory results are preliminary, covering only two related financial tasks, two models, and one primary baseline (ACE); broader evaluations, additional baselines, and repeated runs are needed; retrieval overhead makes individual test queries slower despite lower token usage, motivating embedding-based/hybrid retrievers, caching, and improved graph routing; longer continual-learning streams and cross-model transfer remain untested [2610.02687v1]. CoEM’s limitations are not explicitly stated in the provided content. KV-Kaizen notes that some selectors vary with input and dataset while others return the same configuration across prompts; a budget-conditioned selector serving several compression targets incurs larger training cost; the model must be trained under the configuration used for serving, as applying a learned configuration to a frozen backbone collapses accuracy [2609.37988v2]. Galahad’s limitations are not explicitly stated in the provided content. CMP shows that identified memory utility alone is insufficient for retention decisions because per-query utility does not generalize to unseen queries; the framework assumes irreversible operations and does not address write-time limitations such as contradictory fact accumulation [2610.02070v2].
